rationale: Imports are about 40% of supply and Halvern buys a small share of world steel, so foreign sellers have little reason to absorb most of the tariff and imports should stay a meaningful share.
evidence: Three domestic steel firms supply about 60% of the steel used in Halvern; the rest is imported (WE-013 record).
Halvern buys a small share of the world's steel and has a floating exchange rate (WE-013 record).

rationale: Domestic firms supply about 60% of steel and the exclusion process presumes some products are not produced domestically in sufficient quantity or quality, so close substitutes for most imports are unlikely in the medium run.
evidence: Three domestic steel firms supply about 60% of the steel used in Halvern; the rest is imported (WE-013 record).
The standard for "sufficient quantity or quality" is not defined.

rationale: The floating exchange rate is the kind of adjustment channel that tends to offset part of a tariff-driven fall in imports, so the fall is more likely offset than left unoffset.
evidence: Halvern is a mid-sized trading country with its own currency and a floating exchange rate.

rationale: Steel is a main input for about 4,000 domestic manufacturers, and the record gives no sign of cheap medium-run replacement, so the taxed input is likely hard to replace at the old cost.
evidence: About 4,000 domestic manufacturers use steel as a main input (WE-013 record).

rationale: Imported finished goods containing steel (machinery, vehicles, appliances) are not covered, so steel-using downstream makers compete with sellers who do not face the 25% tariff.
evidence: Imported fabricated steel products and finished goods containing steel (machinery, vehicles, appliances, fabricated structural sections, fasteners) are not covered.
